cues.text: Hello, are you Dr Lindsey? The Returning Students Advisor?
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: Yes, that’s right. Are you Frank? Your appointment wasn’t till 2:00, but that's OK. Please come in and have a seat.
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: Thanks, I like to arrive early whenever I have anything to do.
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: That’s certainly a praiseworthy habit. Let me see, it looks like you’ve taken a long break from school, and I understand you wanted to have a chat about what you should study if and when you return for further classes.
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: It’s such a big challenge. I don’t know if I’m crazy for doing this or not!
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: Believe it or not, I know exactly what you mean. Before I began working here at the university, I taught primary school for nearly ten years. It takes a lot of courage to go back to school!
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: I feel more shy and scared than the primary students I teach! In the schools I taught, I found today’s youngsters are very sure of themselves.
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: In terms of intelligence, I have a lot to teach them. And the maturity level of much of my class leaves something to be desired.
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: But in terms of confidence, wow! A lot more confident than I am now, that’s for sure!
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: Stop fretting. “A brave man is a coward who refuses to run.” Let’s talk about your strong points. You seem an intelligent man. What is it you would like to study?
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: You see, I’ve been teaching children for a few years, but I think I’d be happier teaching adults.
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: I think teaching students in middle school is much more satisfying because they end up being much more grateful for your work. If I may ask, what got you interested in teaching adults?
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: A lot of things, I guess. I met my future wife back in my first year of college. She always complains that I was more interesting then. She says that now I talk like I’m seven years old! That’s probably from being with children all day.
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: Ha ha ha! Again I know just what you mean. My husband used to say the same thing about me when I taught kindergarten. Anything else?
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: Well, yes. Fairly often now I run into former students and we talk. Some of them are getting close to being grown up. I guess I think more and more about how people develop over time. So, I'm interested in the results of education, you know, the final stages.
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: I see. Well, coming back to the university can be both difficult and very rewarding.
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: There are some problems unique to returning students, you know, older students like yourself. What do you think is your greatest weakness?
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: Well, I actually think my confidence is getting better.
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: I’m definitely overcoming my introversion and starting to be much more comfortable in front of a class.
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: To tell the truth, I’m afraid I’m rather behind the times about many things. It’s more difficult for me to chase after the popular things youngsters are fond of - such as Iphone, Twitter, if you name it!
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: I think I understand.
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: How old are you, 35? People at your age still go back to school for further education. I was a bit the same way.
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: I mean I didn’t study at the university till after I had a family: a husband and one child. My point of view was a lot different from your average eighteen-year-old girl’s, I can tell you!
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: Gee, that sounds pretty rough. A family and college?
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: Clearly you weren’t unsuccessful though!
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: It was, Frank. It truly was. My first term at school was extremely stressful. But excuse me! You’re not here to listen to my life story. We’re talking about your plans.
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: Is there anything unique I should know about you or your past experience or plans?
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: I’m afraid not. There is nothing interesting about my career or plans. It’s really not too impressive.
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: Now, I forbid you to talk like that. This is your one life, and if you’re not interested, why bother living it? Don’t be so humble, Frank.
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: OK, OK. My wife says I’m a wimp.
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: Let's talk about your dreams a bit. You want to teach adults, you said. What would you like to teach them?
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: Well, when I first came to college, I really liked Languages and Literature. A lot of people have told me that for practical reasons, it would be more rewarding to choose Business Management as my major, but I made up my mind to study Liberal Arts once I got the idea of going back to school.
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: I must say it’s refreshing to meet someone who knows there’s more to an education than computers and finance. Let’s have a look at the university course catalogue...
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: Excuse me, Dr Lindsey. Before we do that, could I maybe ask you some questions about changes in university life? I think I need to discuss that so I know what to expect.
cues.speaker: FRANK

cues.text: Of course. I’m here to help you. The biggest thing to get used to is the change in technology. Professors present things on huge screens, many of which are interactive computerised whiteboards. You can write on them still and use them like a touch screen. They’re really handy! No more sloppy scribbled notes on the projector. Let's see, I doubt you’ll be living in student housing, so I won’t go into all the improvements there.

cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY

cues.text: As a student, you have 24-hour access to the gym, and library privileges that include the use of school computers to scan, copy, and print, and of course the Media Library, which contains movies from all genres and most of the movies listed on AFI’s Top 100 Movies of All Time. The dining facilities are also not what they used to be.
cues.speaker: DR LINDSEY
